Body Size: Medium-sized nocturnal caprimulgid birds with compact, streamlined overall body outline; body proportions are slender and elongated relative to small passerines, exhibiting a typical cryptic, stocky torso with long wingspan and moderate body mass, uniform medium size across the three species.

Legs and Feet: Short, thin legs with brownish-gray or flesh-toned coloration; feet possess slender, sharp curved claws adapted for perching and ground roosting; no webbing present, anisodactyl foot structure typical of caprimulgids.

Body Size: Small to medium-sized coraciiform kingfishers with a characteristic compact, large-headed, short-necked fusiform body plan and stocky torso. Interspecific size variation is distinct: Belted Kingfisher is the largest and most robust, while Green Kingfisher is the smallest and more delicately proportioned; Pied, Ringed, and White-breasted Kingfishers occupy intermediate body stature. Sexual size dimorphism is minimal; adults exhibit firm, well-defined body contours, whereas juveniles possess slightly slimmer builds with softer, less compact bodily proportions. Body Plumage: Feather texture is dense, sleek, tightly appressed, and water-repellent with smooth layered contour feathering. Adult plumage is dominated by slate blue, metallic iridescent green, crisp black, and immaculate white, frequently patterned with bold dark breast bands, clean white cervical collars, solid hooded crowns, and sharp lateral color demarcation. Non-breeding adults retain core coloration with slightly softened contrast. Juvenile and immature plumage is overall duller, browner-toned, with faint blurred breast banding and reduced iridescence; they lack the crisp boundary definition and full color saturation of definitive adult plumage, attaining mature patterning via gradual molt progression. Beak: Possess an elongated, exceptionally stout, dagger-like triangular bill with a broad basal structure, straight culmen, and sharply pointed apex, morphologically adapted for piscivory. Bill coloration varies across solid black, dusky gray, and pale horn-green tones; the mandible is robust and keratinous, suited for diving strikes, seizing aquatic prey, and probing riparian substrates. Eyes: Iris is uniformly deep dark brown to blackish-brown in all adult, immature, and juvenile individuals; orbital pigmentation is consistent, lacking prominent colored eye rings and maintaining strong tonal contrast against surrounding head plumage. Face: Periorbital and loral regions are fully densely feathered without bare facial skin; feathering at the bill base is tight and smoothly integrated with lores and forehead. Many species develop an erect semi-crested crown, distinct white neck collars, dark facial masks, and solid hooded head patterning. Adult facial markings are sharp and well-demarcated, while juveniles show muted, blurred facial contrast and less defined collar and mask boundaries. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is fine-textured, dense, and neatly layered. Ventral base colors include pure immaculate white, warm rufous, and pale buff; multiple species feature a thick dark pectoral band bisecting the breast, while others display unstreaked, uniformly plain underparts. Juvenile abdomens exhibit faint dusky smudging and washed-out tonalities with indistinct banding compared to the clean, high-contrast ventral patterning of adults; undertail coverts are compact, fluffy, and match ventral ground color. Wings: Wings are moderately short, broad, and rounded with blunt wingtips, adapted for rapid direct flight, stationary hovering over water, and short-range arboreal movement. Upperwing coverts and flight feathers are solid slate blue, iridescent green, or blackish with fine pale feather edging; underwings are plain pale gray or off-white without elaborate wing bars or contrasting patches. Wings fold closely against the streamlined torso when perched. Tail: Medium-short to medium-length tail with square-ended or slightly rounded silhouette; rectrices are rigid and sturdy. Tail coloration aligns with body hues of blue, green, black, and white, often bearing subtle pale terminal margins. Upper tail coverts integrate seamlessly with rump plumage; under tail coverts are soft, compactly layered, and consistent with ventral abdominal coloration. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, delicate, and slender, colored dusky gray or blackish. Feet follow passerine anisodactyl arrangement with three toes forward and one hallux posterior; toes are syndactyl with fused basal segments, equipped with small, sharp, curved keratin claws for gripping riverine branches, snags, and exposed perches. Feet are entirely non-webbed, specialized solely for arboreal perching and riparian stationary surveillance.

Body Size: Small to medium-sized cuculiform birds with elongated, slender body outlines; Geococcyx exhibits notably larger and more robust terrestrial build, while Groove-billed Ani and the three cuckoo species possess compact to moderately slender torsos. All taxa display streamlined proportions with extended neck and torso structure, adults are structurally larger and more proportioned than immature individuals, lacking extreme sexual size dimorphism. Body Plumage: Dominated by matte black, iridescent glossy black, dusky brown, grayish-brown, and soft rufous upperparts across species; feather texture is dense, fine, and loosely textured with subtle metallic iridescence on mantle and wing coverts in adult plumage. Juvenile plumage is duller, muted, with faint barring or buff-edged feather margins, lacking the glossy sheen of breeding adults; adult plumage is uniform and crisp without prominent seasonal mottling. Beak: Bills are moderately stout to robust, decurved or straight with pointed to slightly hooked tips; Groove-billed Ani features a deep, compressed bill with distinct longitudinal grooves on the culmen. Bill color varies from solid black, grayish-black to pale yellow and pale horn; all have sturdy keratin structure adapted for insectivory, occasional frugivory and small vertebrate predation. Eyes: Iris color ranges from deep dark brown to reddish-brown and pale yellowish-white in adult individuals; juveniles often have duller, cloudier dusky irides, with consistent orbital pigmentation across the group. Face: Periorbital region is closely feathered, lacking bare skin lores in most species; bill base is tightly feathered with smooth loral plumage. No bold facial patches present; subtle dusky shading on lores and forehead is observable in some cuckoo taxa, with plain, unpatterned facial contour overall. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is predominantly pale off-white, creamy buff, soft gray, or dull rufous with fine loose feather texture; some species show uniform dark sooty underparts. Juvenile abdomens carry faint fine barring or muted buff wash, while adults present cleaner, more solid coloration without heavy streaking. Wings: Wings are moderately short to medium in length, rounded and slightly concave in shape, adapted for short burst flight and sedentary perching. Upperwing coverts and flight feathers match mantle hues of black, brown or gray; underwings are paler, with soft muted gray or buff-toned plumage, lacking bright contrasting markings. Tail: Exceptionally long, graduated tail with rounded or slightly wedge-shaped silhouette, constituting a major portion of total body length. Tail plumage is glossy black, dark brown or gray with subtle pale terminal spots or faint barring in several species; upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump coloration, under tail coverts are soft-textured, pale buff or dark sooty, neatly layered. Legs and Feet: Legs are slender to moderately robust, medium-length, colored grayish-black, dark brown or flesh gray; zygodactyl foot arrangement typical of cuckoos, with two toes forward and two toes backward. Feet bear sharp, curved keratin claws for gripping branches, trunks and terrestrial substrates; fully non-webbed, adapted for arboreal perching and ground foraging.

Body Size: Medium-small loon species, compact streamlined fusiform body outline; noticeably smaller than Common Loon and Yellow-billed Loon, with a slender neck, rounded chest, and tapered hindbody, exhibiting an elegant aquatic contour adapted for diving and migratory flight. 
Body Plumage: Breeding adult has smooth, glossy blackish-purple head and hindneck with fine greenish iridescence; upperparts dark greyish-black with neatly scaled pale grey feather fringes. Non-breeding adult loses iridescence, displaying dull grey upperparts and pale whitish foreneck. Juvenile plumage is muted dusky brownish-grey above with distinct pale scalloped edging, underparts cleaner white, lacking the adult’s iridescent sheen. 
Beak: Slender, moderately short, dagger-shaped with straight culmen and pointed tip; relatively fine and less stout than larger loon species; breeding and non-breeding adults have dark grey to black bill; juvenile bill is paler grey with a slight bluish hue at the base. 
Eyes: Iris is deep crimson red, vivid and conspicuous against dark facial plumage. 
Face: Periorbital region enveloped in dark iridescent head feathers without a distinct eye ring; lores and bill base unmarked; breeding plumage features a crisp pale grey demarcation line separating dark crown from pale throat, lacking bold spotting or facial patches. 
Abdomen: Abdominal region immaculate clean white with dense, soft, water-resistant downy feather texture; uniformly unstreaked, extending from lower breast to undertail, maintaining plain pale appearance in all age classes. 
Wings: Moderately long, narrow and pointed, built for swift direct flight; upperwing plain dark greyish-black with subtle muted feather margins; underwing pale silvery-grey along coverts, flight feathers dark grey, lacking conspicuous wing bars. 
Tail: Very short, bluntly rounded and wedge-shaped; rectrices dark sooty grey-black; upper tail coverts dark grey with fine pale edging, under tail coverts blend into white abdominal plumage, compact and tightly feathered. 
Legs and Feet: Legs short, compressed laterally, dark grey to bluish-grey in color; fully webbed palmate feet with strong, pointed curved claws; positioned far posterior on the body, specialized for underwater propulsion and limited awkward terrestrial locomotion.

Body Size: Encompasses small to large-sized passerine birds across multiple families including Parulidae, Passerellidae, Cardinalidae, Icteridae, Corvidae, Hirundinidae, Troglodytidae, Tyrannidae, Vireonidae, Fringillidae, Mimidae, and Alaudidae. Overall body outlines vary from compact petite fusiform frames in warblers, kinglets, and small sparrows; plump rounded silhouettes in finches, waxwings, and grosbeaks; slender streamlined builds in swallows, orioles, and flycatchers; to large robust bulky proportions in crows, ravens, jays, and nutcrackers. Sexual size dimorphism is subtle to moderate; adult individuals exhibit firmer, more proportioned body contours, while juveniles and immatures are slimmer with softer, less defined torso and limb proportions. Body Plumage: Feather texture ranges from dense soft downy, sleek tightly appressed, coarse stiff, to smooth velvety finishes, all with matte or subtle non-iridescent luster, adapted for terrestrial, arboreal, and aerial lifestyles. Adult breeding plumage displays highly diverse saturated hues including vivid yellow, scarlet, indigo, cerulean, green, rufous, chestnut, solid black, gray, and crisp white, adorned with streaks, bars, hoods, masks, wing bars, crown stripes, and breast patches. Non-breeding adults show muted washed-out tonalities with softened contrasting markings. Juvenile and immature plumage is predominantly cryptic olive-brown, buff, dusky gray, and dull brown, with blurred mottling, faint streaking, and reduced patterning; they lack the sharp color contrast, saturated pigmentation, and definitive ornamental markings of mature adults, acquiring full adult plumage via sequential seasonal molts. Beak: Bill morphology is highly diversified yet functionally grouped: slender pointed attenuated insectivorous bills in warblers, vireos, flycatchers, creepers, and wrens; short thick robust conical seed-cracking bills in sparrows, buntings, finches, grosbeaks, and towhees; moderately long slightly hooked robust corvid-type bills in crows, ravens, jays, and nutcrackers; small delicate triangular bills in swallows and pipits; and stout slightly decurved bills in mimids and shrikes. Bill coloration spans dusky black, grayish horn, pale flesh, yellow, pinkish-brown, and bluish-gray; all structurally specialized for insectivory, granivory, frugivory, omnivory, and occasional predation. Eyes: Iris is uniformly deep dark brown to blackish-brown across nearly all species in adult, immature, and juvenile stages; a small number of corvids and vireos retain consistent dark orbital pigmentation with no prominent contrasting colored eye rings or multi-toned irides as a collective trait. Juvenile irides are slightly duller and faintly clouded compared to the crisp saturated dark irides of adults. Face: Periorbital and loral regions are fully densely feathered without bare facial skin across the entire assemblage; bill base is closely feathered with smooth plumage transition. Facial ornamentation is diverse, including distinct supercilia, eye-lines, dark auricular patches, malar streaks, solid hoods, throat patches, erectile crown crests, and plain unpatterned facial planes. Adult facial markings are sharp, well-demarcated, and high-contrast; females and juveniles exhibit blurred subdued facial patterning with softened boundary definition and reduced tonal contrast. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage features fine dense soft feather texture, with base coloration covering immaculate white, creamy buff, pale gray, bright yellow, rufous, olive, and dusky brown. Many taxa display clean unstreaked underparts, fine dark longitudinal streaks, centralized breast smudges, or bold colored breast bands. Juveniles and immatures show paler washed-out abdominal tones with heavier indistinct mottling and streaking; undertail coverts are voluminous, fluffy, neatly layered, and match ventral base plumage in pale buff, white, or muted earthy tones. Wings: Wing morphology adapts to ecological niche: short rounded compact wings in wrens, sparrows, warblers, and mimids for short burst flight and arboreal gleaning; long narrow pointed wings in swallows, corvids, and orioles for sustained aerial flight and soaring; moderately broad rounded wings in grosbeaks, buntings, and blackbirds. Upperwing coverts and remiges are mottled brown, gray, olive, and blackish, frequently marked with pale or rufous wing bars, fine pale feather edging, and concealed marginal patterns. Underwings are plain pale gray, buff, or white with compact layered feather structure, lacking overly elaborate bold contrasting markings. Tail: Tail length ranges from short compact to notably elongated; shape includes square-tipped, rounded, slightly notched, deeply forked, graduated, and wedge-shaped silhouettes. Rectrix coloration matches body plumage in black, gray, brown, olive, yellow, and rufous, with many species bearing pale terminal spots or subtle barring. Upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump plumage; under tail coverts are soft-textured, compactly layered, and harmonize with ventral abdominal coloration across all taxa. Legs and Feet: Legs vary from short delicate to moderately sturdy medium length, with coloration of dusky gray, pinkish-brown, flesh tone, blackish, and dark brown. All species possess standard passerine anisodactyl foot arrangement (three toes forward, one posterior hallux); equipped with well-developed sharp curved keratin claws adapted for gripping tree twigs, shrub stems, rocky substrates, grass stalks, and ground litter. Feet are completely non-webbed, specialized for arboreal perching, terrestrial hopping, ground foraging, clinging to vertical bark, and open-country locomotion.

Body Size: Large to very large pelecaniform waterbirds with massive, robust torso, broad chest, and bulky overall body outline; both species possess an elongated neck, large rounded head, and heavy-set proportions typical of pelicans; White_Pelican is marginally bulkier and taller than Brown_Pelican, sharing the same oversized aquatic bird body architecture with wide wingspans and compact abdominal girth. 
Body Plumage: Adult plumage presents species-specific base tones of immaculate white or muted dusky brownish-gray; feather texture is dense, coarse, and densely layered with waterproof contour feathers and soft downy underplumage for aquatic insulation; juveniles of both species exhibit duller, mottled grayish-brown plumage with faded, less saturated tones, lacking the crisp clean coloration of breeding adults, and show looser, fluffier feather texture until full maturation. 
Beak: Exceptionally long, stout, and massively robust with an elongated mandible and a prominent expandable throat pouch attached to the lower bill; culmen slightly decurved with a distinct hooked nail at the tip; bill color varies with species and breeding season but maintains the same oversized, thick-based structural morphology adapted for plunge diving and fish capture. 
Eyes: Moderately small relative to head size, rounded in shape; iris displays pale yellow, pale amber, or deep brown hues, consistent with pelican visual adaptation for aquatic and aerial foraging. 
Face: Periorbital region features bare, unfeathered facial skin with variable pale pink, orange, or grayish pigmentation; lores and bill base are largely devoid of dense plumage; both species lack bold patterned facial patches, characterized by smooth bare facial lores and gular pouch continuity with the lower mandible. 
Abdomen: Ventral plumage is either pure white or muted gray-brown with thick, compact feather texture; abdominal contour is full and rounded; underpart feathers are dense and water-repellent, with juveniles showing faint dusky mottling across the abdomen compared to uniform adult ventral coloration. 
Wings: Extremely long, broad, and paddle-shaped with deeply curved trailing margins; flight feathers are robust and elongated, adapted for dynamic soaring and gliding over open water; wing plumage is solid white or dark brownish-gray with contrasting black primary remiges in both species; folded wings lay flat against the bulky torso. 
Tail: Short, stubby, and broadly rounded in shape; rectrices are stiff and compact with uniform pale white or dusky gray-brown coloration; upper tail coverts align closely with dorsal body plumage, while under tail coverts are softer, paler, and densely downy in texture. 
Legs and Feet: Short, thick, sturdy legs with grayish, pinkish, or orange skin tone; feet are fully totipalmate with complete webbing connecting all four toes; claws are short, thick, and blunt, adapted for swimming, floating on water surfaces, and stable terrestrial perching on shorelines.

Body Size: Small to large piciform woodpeckers with an elongated, rigid upright body silhouette, stiff posture, and sturdy neck structure. Pileated Woodpecker is markedly the largest and most robust; Downy Woodpecker the smallest and most compact; Northern Flicker, Red-headed, Red-bellied, Red-cockaded, and American Three-toed Woodpeckers fall into intermediate medium body proportions. Sexual size dimorphism is slight; adults have firmer, more angular body contours, while juveniles appear slightly slimmer with softer, less rigid overall outlines. Body Plumage: Feather texture is dense, stiff, compact, and tightly appressed, with reinforced contour feathers adapted for impact absorption during trunk hammering. Adult plumage combines base tones of black, white, brown, gray, and barred buff, accented by bold red crowns, nape patches, facial markings, and solid monochromatic head coloration. Many species feature distinct horizontal barring, vertical spotting, or clean unmarked patches across mantle and underparts. Juvenile and immature plumage is duller, muted, with blurred barring, reduced red pigmentation, and lack of crisp adult head markings; they attain full adult coloration and patterning through successive annual molts. Beak: Chisel-shaped, robust, elongated bill with straight culmen, broad sturdy base, and sharp pointed cutting tip; structurally reinforced for excavating bark, drilling wood, and probing insect larvae. Bill stoutness varies interspecifically: larger species possess thicker, longer bills, while smaller woodpeckers have shorter, more delicate chisels. Bill color ranges from solid dusky black, grayish horn to pale slate; keratin texture is dense and wear-resistant. Eyes: Iris is uniformly deep dark brown to blackish-brown across all adults, immatures, and juveniles; orbital area is well-defined, with consistent pigmentation and no prominent eye rings, maintaining strong contrast against facial plumage patches. Face: Periorbital region is fully densely feathered without bare skin; lores and bill base are closely feathered with tight plumage integration. The group exhibits diagnostic facial traits including bright red crowns, nape crescent patches, small red cockades, solid red full heads, dark facial masks, and plain unpatterned lores. Adult facial markings are sharp and well-demarcated; juveniles show faded red accents, blurred boundaries, and absent or reduced nuptial head patches. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is dense, firm, and neatly layered; base coloration spans clean white, creamy buff, pale gray, tawny brown, and warm tan. Several species display fine dark spotting, bold barring, or uniform unstreaked ventral plumage. Juvenile abdomens carry muted washed-out tones with softer, less defined spotting and barring compared to the crisply patterned underparts of adults; undertail coverts are compact, stiff-textured, and match ventral ground color. Wings: Moderately long, broad, and rounded wing shape adapted for bounding undulating flight and short-distance arboreal movement. Upperwing coverts and remiges are patterned with black, white, brown, and buff barring or solid dark tones; flight feathers are sturdy and reinforced. Underwings are plain pale buff or gray with neat layered feather structure, lacking extravagant contrasting patterns. Tail: Medium-length, stiff, wedge-shaped tail with rigid pointed rectrices specialized as a prop for vertical trunk clinging. Tail plumage features black, dark brown, and white barring or solid dark coloration. Upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump plumage; under tail coverts are short, dense, and tightly arranged, supporting stable vertical perching posture. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, sturdy, and muscular, colored dusky gray or blackish. Feet exhibit zygodactyl arrangement with two toes forward and two toes backward; equipped with large, sharply curved, robust keratin claws adapted for gripping tree bark, trunks, and vertical wooden substrates. Feet are entirely non-webbed, perfectly specialized for arboreal climbing, trunk clinging, and upright foraging posture.

Body Size: Small to medium-sized aquatic grebes of Podicipedidae, possessing a compact, streamlined, fusiform body with a notably low-slung torso adapted for aquatic diving. Western Grebe is markedly larger and more elongated than the smaller Eared Grebe, Horned Grebe, and Pied-billed Grebe. All species exhibit rounded chest and tapered hindquarters; sexual size dimorphism is minimal, adults appear fuller and more robust, while juveniles are slimmer with a more delicate overall silhouette. Body Plumage: Feather texture is exceptionally dense, silky, waterproof, and tightly furled, providing superior insulation and buoyancy. Basic non-breeding plumage is dominated by dark dusky gray, blackish upperparts and clean white to pale gray underparts; breeding adults develop rich saturated rusty rufous, black, and golden ornamental head plumes and intensified tonal contrast. Juvenile plumage is muted pale gray and off-white with duller, washed-out upperpart tones, lacking the vibrant breeding coloration and elaborate head filoplumes of mature adults; plumage is non-iridescent with smooth layering across mantle and flanks. Beak: Bill is moderately short to elongated, slender to moderately stout, sharply pointed with straight culmen and fine tip; Pied-billed Grebe has a shorter, thicker, more robust conical bill, while the other three species feature slender, attenuated piscivorous bills. Bill color ranges from dusky gray, black, pale horn to vivid yellow; some species display distinct pale bands or dark pigmentation on the mandible, structurally adapted for capturing aquatic invertebrates and small fish. Eyes: Iris is predominantly bright crimson red, deep ruby, or dark reddish-brown in adult individuals; juveniles possess duller brownish irides with less intense saturation. Orbital area is well-defined, with eye contrast prominent against surrounding head plumage across all taxa. Face: Periorbital region is densely feathered, closely appressed to the eye; lores and bill base are fully feathered without bare skin. Breeding adults develop distinctive erectile golden, buff, or black head crests, ear tufts, and solid dark facial hoods; non-breeding and juvenile individuals have plain, unadorned facial plumage with subdued tonal transition between crown, cheek, and peripheral areas, lacking ornamental plumes. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is dense, soft, and downy-textured, predominantly immaculate white or pale silvery gray in non-breeding adults; breeding individuals may show rufous or dusky smudging on lower flanks. Juvenile abdomens are off-white with faint grayish mottling, presenting a less crisp demarcation between upperparts and underparts compared to adults; ventral feathering is highly compact and water-repellent. Wings: Short, narrow, and relatively pointed wing shape, optimized for underwater maneuvering rather than sustained flight. Upperwing coverts and remiges are uniform dark gray or blackish, with inconspicuous pale edging absent in most individuals. Wings are tightly folded against the streamlined body when at rest; underwings are pale gray or whitish with subtle layered feather structure, lacking bold wing bars or contrasting patches. Tail: Extremely short, inconspicuous, rounded tail with compact, fluffy rectrices, appearing nearly tailless in profile. Tail plumage is dark gray or blackish, blending seamlessly with the rump. Upper tail coverts are dark and tightly layered; under tail coverts are voluminous, soft, and white or pale gray, merging smoothly with ventral abdominal plumage. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, robust, positioned far posterior on the torso for aquatic propulsion, colored dusky gray or blackish. Feet are uniquely lobate-webbed with individual lobed membranes on each toe, rather than full webbing; equipped with small, sharp, curved dark keratin claws. Fully adapted for diving, underwater locomotion, and shallow wetland foraging, unsuited for terrestrial walking.

Body Size: Black-footed_Albatross (50–60 cm) exhibits a robust, streamlined body with a slightly shorter overall outline compared to Sooty_Albatross; Laysan_Albatross (45–55 cm) is more slender and compact; Sooty_Albatross (60–70 cm) has a notably larger, more robust build with a longer wingspan relative to body mass; Northern_Fulmar (30–40 cm) is the smallest species with a compact, dense body structure and a shorter overall outline than all albatrosses.  
Body Plumage: Black-footed_Albatross adults display dark gray-brown upperparts with fine blackish streaks on the flanks, while underparts are pale gray with distinct blackish streaking; juveniles are uniformly brownish-gray with less defined streaking. Laysan_Albatross adults have a pale gray body with a distinct white head and dark cap, contrasting with pale underparts; juveniles are brownish with white patches on the throat and flanks. Sooty_Albatross adults are uniformly sooty gray across the body with minimal variation; juveniles are paler gray-brown with faint streaking. Northern_Fulmar adults feature a black head and dark brown neck, with white underparts and dark streaks on the flanks; juveniles are brownish with pale underparts and less defined markings.  
Beak: Black-footed_Albatross has a black, moderately hooked beak with a slightly curved tip; Laysan_Albatross has a dark gray, slender beak with a fine, pointed tip; Sooty_Albatross has a black, robust beak with a strong, slightly hooked tip; Northern_Fulmar has a dark gray, slightly hooked beak with a blunt tip.  
Eyes: All species exhibit dark brown irises.  
Face: Black-footed_Albatross has a dark brown periorbital area with minimal visible patches; Laysan_Albatross has a dark cap over the eyes with a pale orbital region; Sooty_Albatross has a dark brown periorbital area with no distinct patches; Northern_Fulmar has a dark brown periorbital area with a pale orbital region.  
Abdomen: Black-footed_Albatross has a pale gray abdomen with fine blackish streaks; Laysan_Albatross has a pale gray abdomen with minimal streaking; Sooty_Albatross has a dark gray abdomen with smooth texture; Northern_Fulmar has a smooth, white abdomen with no streaking.  
Wings: Black-footed_Albatross has long, narrow wings with a dark gray upper surface and pale underwings; Laysan_Albatross has long, narrow wings with pale gray upper surfaces and pale underwings; Sooty_Albatross has long, narrow wings with dark gray upper surfaces and pale underwings; Northern_Fulmar has short, rounded wings with dark gray upper surfaces and pale underwings.  
Tail: Black-footed_Albatross has a long, graduated tail with dark gray upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts; Laysan_Albatross has a short, square tail with dark gray upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts; Sooty_Albatross has a long, graduated tail with dark gray upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts; Northern_Fulmar has a short, rounded tail with dark gray upper tail coverts and pale under tail coverts.  
Legs and Feet: All species have non-webbed feet with sharp, pointed claws; no webbing is present on any foot.

Body Size: Medium to large marine seabirds encompassing three cormorant species and frigatebirds, possessing elongated, streamlined fusiform body contours with long necks and balanced torso proportions. Among cormorants, Brandt Cormorant is the largest and bulkiest, Red-faced Cormorant intermediate, and Pelagic Cormorant the smallest and most slender; frigatebirds exhibit exceptionally lightweight, graceful aerodynamic builds with greatly extended wingspans far exceeding body mass. Sexual size dimorphism is slight to moderate; adult individuals show firmer, more robust body framing, while juveniles have slimmer, softer overall silhouettes. Body Plumage: Feather texture is dense, stiff, tightly packed, and water-resistant in cormorants, while frigatebirds bear lighter, softer, loosely structured contour feathers optimized for prolonged soaring. Adult breeding plumage is dominated by deep glossy black, charcoal, and iridescent bluish-green tones across cormorants; frigatebirds display uniform jet-black adult plumage with vivid colored ventral gular patches in males. Non-breeding adults retain dark base hues with subdued iridescence and lack nuptial ornamental plumes. Juvenile and immature individuals of all taxa exhibit dull sooty brown, dusky gray, and matte dark brown plumage with faint pale underpart mottling, lacking the intense metallic iridescence and saturated bare-skin facial coloration of definitive adults. Beak: Bills are moderately long to elongated, robust at the base and tapering distally; cormorants feature sharply hooked tomial tips adapted for piscivory, with distinct nasal grooves along the culmen. Frigatebirds possess a slender, pointed, slightly decurved bill with a subtle terminal hook. Bill coloration ranges from dusky gray, blackish, and pale horn to vivid reddish or yellowish pigmentation at the basal region in breeding adults; overall keratin structure is sturdy for seizing aquatic prey and surface foraging. Eyes: Adult iris exhibits deep emerald green, turquoise, or dark brownish-green pigmentation in cormorants, while frigatebirds have dark brown to blackish irides with consistent solid tone. Juvenile irides are duller, muted dark brown with reduced chromatic saturation, lacking the bright iris contrast seen in mature breeding individuals. Face: Periorbital, loral, and bill-base regions feature prominent bare, unfeathered facial skin in all taxa, displaying vivid red, carmine, or dusky tonalities during breeding condition. Cormorants develop delicate filamentous head plumes in nuptial plumage; frigatebirds possess a large inflatable colored gular sac beneath the mandible as a key facial characteristic. Non-breeding and juvenile individuals have duller, desaturated bare facial skin and lack ornamental plumes or inflated gular sac morphology. Abdomen: Abdominal plumage is dense, stiff, and closely appressed in cormorants, uniformly glossy black or dark sooty gray with continuous iridescent blending from breast to vent. Frigatebirds have soft, lightweight ventral feathering, mostly black with striking contrasting scarlet or white abdominal/gular markings in sex-specific morphs. Juvenile abdomens show muted brownish-black or pale gray mottling with a matte finish, lacking the sleek iridescence and crisp color demarcation of adults; undertail coverts are compact, densely layered, and match ventral base tones. Wings: Wings are exceptionally long, broad, and pointed across the assemblage; cormorant wings are sturdy for diving propulsion and coastal flight, while frigatebirds have extremely elongated, narrow wings specialized for dynamic oceanic soaring and effortless gliding. Upperwing coverts and remiges are solid glossy black or dark charcoal with subtle iridescent greenish-blue sheen; underwings are plain dark sooty gray without bold patches or wing bars. Wings fold tightly against the torso when perched or resting on water. Tail: Cormorants have moderately long, wedge-shaped or graduated stiff rectrices with dark uniform plumage. Frigatebirds possess a deeply forked, elongated tail with sharply tapered outer rectrices, a defining silhouette trait. Upper tail coverts blend seamlessly with rump dark plumage; under tail coverts are short, dense, and uniformly dark, maintaining streamlined ventral contouring in all species. Legs and Feet: Legs are short, sturdy, and positioned posteriorly on the torso in cormorants, colored dark gray, black, or fleshy red in breeding adults; frigatebirds have extremely short, delicate legs unsuited for terrestrial locomotion. Cormorants have fully totipalmate webbed feet with four interconnected toes and strong curved keratin claws for cliff clinging and aquatic propulsion. Frigatebirds have small, weakly webbed feet with sharp curved claws, adapted only for perching; all taxa are non-specialized for terrestrial walking, with feet fully adapted to marine perching, soaring, and aquatic habitats.
